clinical_knowledge.topic: Tricuspid Valve Endocarditis (IV drug use) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Tricuspid Valve Endocarditis (IV drug use) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management requires prolonged IV antibiotics targeted to blood culture results (empiric coverage for Staphylococcus aureus, the most common organism in IVDU-associated tricuspid endocarditis) and surgical evaluation when there is persistent bacteremia, recurrent septic emboli, or right heart failure.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: high fever, septic pulmonary emboli with cavitary lung lesions, and right-sided heart murmur

Key HPI features: 33M active IV methamphetamine user presenting with bacteremia, bilateral nodular cavitary lung infiltrates, and TEE showing 2 cm vegetation on tricuspid valve requiring repair/replacement.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Tricuspid Valve Endocarditis IV Drug Use.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Tricuspid Valve Endocarditis (IV drug use).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Left-sided (aortic/mitral) endocarditis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Respiratory distress with new cavitary lesions — signals ongoing septic embolization.
management_principles: Start empiric IV antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin) after blood cultures are drawn, then narrow therapy once the causative organism and sensitivities are known
Consult cardiothoracic surgery and infectious disease; counsel on harm-reduction and substance-use treatment referral
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Bacteria introduced through injection drug use seed the tricuspid valve, and vegetation fragments embolize to the lungs, causing septic pulmonary emboli with cavitary lesions and fever.
red_flags: Respiratory distress with new cavitary lesions — signals ongoing septic embolization

must_ask.say: Can you tell me about your drug use — what and how often you inject?
How long have you had fevers?
Any cough, chest pain, or coughing up blood?
Have you had any skin infections at your injection sites?
Have you had a heart valve infection before?
